Ad hunc porro modum definite pronuntio, Deum per Seraphim ac per Trisagium hymnum unam in tribus hypostasibus divinitatem ac dominationem tanquam per arithmeticam quamdam declarationem Isaiæ revelasse. Cur enim non bis, aut quater, aut sexcenties vocem hanc Sanctus cecinerunt? Quid item est, cur nec bis, nec ter, aut quater, aut sexcenties, hæc verba, Dominus Sabaoth, pleni sunt cœli et terra gloria ejus, pronuntiarunt, verum vocem Sanctus ter, vocabulum autem Dominus semel duntaxat Seraphim exclamarunt? unplaced.en: Damascene says the same in his letter to Jordan the archimandrite, On the Trisagion hymn, ch. 2 (Works vol. 1, p. 483; new edition vol. 2; this Patrology vol. 95, col. 27). Editor: In this way he defines the matter: God, through the Seraphim and through the Trisagion hymn, revealed to Isaiah one divinity and dominion in three hypostases, as by a kind of arithmetical declaration. And why did they not pronounce the words 'Lord Sabaoth, heaven and earth are full of his glory' neither twice nor three times nor four times nor six hundred times, but sing the word Holy three times and the name Lord only once? Was it not to show that the holy hypostases are indeed three, but the dominion one, the rule one, the glory one, and one essence and Godhead?

Hoc porro nihil est aliud quam Filium, juxta Arii furorem, a Patris sanctique Spiritus substantia sejungere, eumque inducere alterius substantiæ; aut, sin minus hoc, at perinde est ac negare, juxta Nestorii blasphemiam, Christum esse Deum unumque sanctæ Trinitatis; at idem est ac quartæ cuidam personæ, secundum illorum dementiam, hunc hymnum deferre: non pervidentes, se per id, quo honorem Filio tribuere se existimant, eumdem inhonorare, ipsumque ab adoratione, quæ Patri ac Spiritui sancto defertur, separare.

unplaced.en: Pope Felix III had already reproached Peter the Fuller with the same (letter 4), saying: Sometimes you say that the Trinity was crucified for us, not Christ, etc. Then the pontiff adds, by which the heretic might recover himself: Sometimes ... you have come to something worse ... by referring the whole hymn to the Son. On this it may help to cite what the emperor Justinian argues against Severus in his tract Against the Monophysites, published in Greek by Angelo Mai (Nova Collectio vol. 7, p. 311; this Patrology vol. 86, col. 1103. Editor): For Severus even dared to say that the Trisagion hymn is referred to the Son alone, the Father and the Holy Spirit being excluded from the doxology. But this is nothing other than to sunder the Son, after the madness of Arius, from the substance of the Father and the Holy Spirit and to bring in a different substance; or, failing that, it is the same as to deny, after the blasphemy of Nestorius, that Christ is God and one of the holy Trinity; or it is the same as to attribute this hymn to a fourth person, according to their madness: not seeing that through that by which they think to give honour to the Son they dishonour him, and separate him from the adoration offered to the Father and the Holy Spirit.

How could any creature not be conceived purer than the Virgin Mother of God?

unplaced.anchorLine: quoniam et præ omnibus creaturis (18)
unplaced.en: In what sense the words of Gabriel to the Virgin in St Luke were understood in the Church, behold St Sophronius also comes as a witness. He must be understood to mean the sum of divine gifts bestowed on Mary, so that whatever you may know of, or imagine, granted to other creatures must be held far below the graces with which the holy Virgin was most nobly adorned. Yet no one is unaware that not only the heavenly spirits but also the first parents of the human race came forth adorned by sanctifying grace from the divine hands of the Creator. How then do the prerogatives of all creatures yield to the nobler prerogatives of the Virgin, if, as regards origin, she is to surpass all others, and her origin is to be called splendid by an infinite interval, not only beyond the holy angels, not only beyond the first parents, but even beyond that of the devil and his angels?

Od. α΄): Verbum suprema Deitatis majestate fulgens (et) carnis prius expers, tu, o undequaque sancta, peperisti carne indutum. A sæculo enim tu sola, o purissima ab omni macula, propter micantes puritatis radios, et propter pulchritudinem virginitatis, et propter charismata quamlibet labeculam repellentia, digna apparuisti. (Σεσαρκωμένον. Πανάγια, τέτοκας τὸν πρὶν ἀσώματον θεαρχικὸν Λόγον· μόνη ἐξ αἰῶνος γὰρ ἀκτίσι καθαρότητος, παρθενίας τε κάλλει, καὶ πανάμωμοις χαρίσμασι πέφηνας ἀξία, πανάμωμε.) V, p. 245), monens eam esse vim dictionis, ut nihil sublimius dici queat: Οὐκ ἂν ὀρθῶς εἴποιμεν εἶναί τι ὑπέρτερον.
unplaced.anchorLine: quoniam et digna exstitisti, quæ tantorum magnalium potireris (23), et cœleste ex te gaudium
unplaced.en: Here you have Sophronius voting on his own account with the common opinion of the holy Fathers, who affirm that Mary was worthy, being chosen as mother of God. It is well known that this bears chiefly on her most singular purity. On this it may help to set before the eyes what we read in the liturgical prayers of the Greek Church (Menaion, 12 February, Ode 1): 'Word shining in the supreme majesty of the Godhead and previously without flesh, you, wholly holy one, bore him clothed in flesh. For from the age you alone, most pure, free of every stain, appeared worthy by the shining rays of purity, the beauty of virginity, and gifts that repel any blemish.' (Greek: 'All-holy, you have borne the formerly bodiless Word of the Godhead ...; for alone from eternity by untouched rays of purity, by beauty of virginity and by all-blameless gifts you have shown yourself worthy, all-blameless one.') On the word θεαρχικόν, which recurs in this canon, one should read what Eustathius of Thessalonica notes (Commentary on the Pentecost hymns of Damascene, no. 82; Spicilegium Romanum vol. 5, p. 245), warning that the force of the term is such that nothing loftier can be said: 'We could not rightly say there is anything higher.'

unplaced.text: Inducitur hic Gabriel gratiam sanctæ Virgini divinitus collatam miris efferens encomiis, et per hæc ejusdem animum confirmans, ne scilicet deplorandum primæ matris Evæ lapsum sibi quoque metuat. Eam autem in rem archangelus tacite comparationem quamdam inter Mariæ atque Evæ gratiam instituit, et duplici ex capite gratiam Deiparæ tanquam præstantiorem celebrat. Ac primo quidem illud utriusque gratiæ discrimen attingit, quod ad illum sanctæ Virginis metum eximendum pressius facit, et temporariæ gratiæ protogenitricis (hæc enim a congenita sibi gratia cito excidit), stabilem Mariæ gratiam opponit, quam propterea ἀθάνατον, ἀμείωτον, σωτήριον, ἀκλόνητον, ἀσάλευτον, ἀνίκητον, atque αἴδιον appellat: quæ quidem inviete præterea ostendunt, quam vetus, quamque explorata fuerit in Ecclesia doctrina, qua traditur sanctissimam Dei Genitricem in gratia confirmatam fuisse. Deinde vero nonnulla alia interserit, quæ universim ad ejusdem gratiæ præcellentiam prædicandam spectant, uti cum eam dicit ὑπέρλαμπρον, πολύευκτον, ὑπέρφωτον. Porro facillime patet, gratiam Deiparæ haud ὑπέρλαμπρον, aut ὑπέρφωτον, aut πολύευκτον præ gratia Evæ dici posse, nisi Evæ consortem Deiparam in eo statuas, quod ad primam spectat originem. Quid enim æquiparari illi gratiæ potest, quæ efficiat, ut nunquam non charissima Deo anima exstiterit, nunquam non cœlesti illa claritate refulserit? Quænam gratia majori pretio habenda ac potiori exoptanda affectu, quam quæ impediat, ne inter prima existendi initia anima Deo invisa, diabolo mancipata, in se turpissima fuerit?
unplaced.anchorLine: Deum gratiam perennitèr duraturam (24.)
unplaced.en: Here Gabriel is introduced extolling with wondrous praises the grace divinely conferred on the holy Virgin, and by these words strengthening her spirit, lest she fear for herself the lamentable fall of the first mother Eve. To this end the archangel tacitly draws a comparison between the grace of Mary and that of Eve, and celebrates the Mother of God's grace as superior on two counts. First he touches on that difference between the two graces: to remove the holy Virgin's fear he puts more pointedly against the temporary grace of the first mother (for she quickly fell from the grace innate to her) the stable grace of Mary, which he therefore calls immortal, undiminished, saving, unshakable, immovable, invincible and eternal; these things moreover show how ancient and how well proven in the Church was the doctrine that the most holy Mother of God was confirmed in grace. Then he inserts several other epithets that bear generally on proclaiming the excellence of that grace, as when he calls it exceedingly bright, much-desired, exceedingly luminous. Moreover it is quite clear that the Mother of God's grace could not be called more brilliant, or more luminous, or more desired than Eve's grace unless you place the Mother of God as Eve's equal in this: as regards first origin. For what can be put on a level with that grace which brings it about that the soul was never not most dear to God and never failed to shine with that heavenly radiance? What grace should be held at greater price and desired with greater longing than that which prevents the soul, in the first beginnings of existence, from being hateful to God, enslaved to the devil, and in itself most foul?

unplaced.text: Comparatio igitur a Sophronio instituta gratiam exsistentiæ coævam in Maria non minus quam in prima matre Eva, astruit, imo præsumit.
unplaced.en: The comparison drawn by Sophronius therefore asserts, indeed presupposes, a grace coeval with existence in Mary no less than in the first mother Eve.

unplaced.text: Merito quæri hic potest, quid sibi velit sanctus Sophronius, cum inquit, Virginem Mariam purificante gratia præoccupatam fuisse, seu magis ῥητῶς Virginem (utique ope gratiæ) præmundatam fuisse. Nam si generatim sermo esset de gratia humanam voluntatem præveniente, sane obvius foret sensus, atque ad illud fidei dogma proposi-tio referenda esset, quo adversus hæreticos Pelagianos ac Semipelagianos profitemur, gratiam divinam humanis meritis non rependi, sed eamdem prævenire humanum quodlibet non modo opus bonum, sed etiam desiderium, ipsumque credulitatis affectum. At enim liquido apparet sancti doctoris sententiam nullatenus huc spectare posse. Ut enim reliqua prætermittamus, quis non videat, Sophronium singularem aliquam Deiparæ prærogativam celebrare his verbis voluisse? Porro quod eo sensu quisquam Dei gratia præoccupetur, adeo singulare dici non debet, ut hæreticus audiat, quisquis affirmet, aut exstitisse unquam aut exsistere quempiam posse hominem gratia exornatum, quem hac ratione gratia non prævenerit: alioquin, ut inquit Apostolus (Rom. XI, 6), gratia jam non est gratia. Sententia igitur sancti Sophronii, ad quidpiam aliud est referenda, quod et capax sit purificationis per gratiam, quodque purificatio ipsa præ-vertere vero aliquo sensu dicatur. At vero tale aliquid evidentissime habes in ipsa humana Deiparæ natura. Purificationis enim non capax modo, sed et indiga per se in præsenti conditione, est humana natura, quippe in primo parente vitiata: tum autem etiam prævertere naturam purificatio rectissime dicitur, cum gratia purificans non jam inductam delet culpam, sed ne induci-tur antevertendo impedit. Et hunc quidem sensum ipsa Sophronii verba important. Singularis enim Virginis prærogativa in eo statuitur, quod ipsa præpurgata fuerit (προκεκάθαρται), dum cæteri Adæ filii non præpurgari, sed purgari dicuntur. At quodnam demum discrimen inter purgatum et præpurgatum reperias, nisi quod illic maculam purgatio subsequitur, ut eam auferat, hic prævenit, ne inficiat? Singulare igitur privilegium quod eo loci Sophronius de beata Dei Matre deprædicat, nullum est aliud, quam singularissima ejusdem ab originali infectione præservatio. Sed et dignissimus, qui consideretur, est totus hujus loci contextus. Sophronius enim, uti liquet, ad instar cujusdam principii, e quo deinde tot tantasque Deiparæ prærogativas deducat, præmittit illud, quod ex Evangelio constat, Mariam plenam gratia fuisse. Ac rursus horum magnalium quasi rationem postea redditurus, gratiæ plenitudinem iterum inculcat, cui subnectit immensum illum munerum divinorum cumulum, quo Deipara munera cuivis creaturæ collata infinito intervallo excedit. Palam est ergo, ex mente SS. Patrum tum in ea gratiæ plenitudine, tum in illo donorum divinorum præ omnibus excessu, et munus illud, angelis et protoparentibus commune, contineri, vi cujus gratia divina ipsi exsistendi initio coæva profitenda sit.
unplaced.anchorLine: purificante gratia præoccupatus es (25);
unplaced.en: One may rightly ask here what St Sophronius means when he says that the Virgin Mary was forestalled by purifying grace, or rather, expressly, that the Virgin was (by the power of grace) pre-cleansed. For if the discussion were about grace in general preceding the human will, the sense would be obvious and would refer to the dogma of faith we profess against the Pelagians and Semipelagians: that divine grace is not repaid for human merits, but precedes every human work, good deed, desire, and even the movement of belief. But it is plainly evident that the holy doctor's thought cannot look to this. To set aside the rest, who does not see that Sophronius meant by these words to celebrate some singular prerogative of the Mother of God? Moreover, that someone be forestalled by God's grace in that sense must not be called so singular that a heretic would be heard, whoever would affirm that there ever was or could be a man adorned with grace whom grace did not precede in this way: otherwise, as the Apostle says (Rom. 11:6), grace is no longer grace. The thought of St Sophronius must therefore refer to something else, which is capable of purification by grace and which purification itself may in some sense be said to forestall. And you have such a thing most evidently in the Mother of God's human nature itself. Human nature, being in the first parent vitiated, is not only capable of purification but in its present condition needs it of itself; and purification is most rightly said to forestall nature when purifying grace does not remove a guilt already incurred but prevents its being incurred by acting in advance. And Sophronius's very words import this sense. The Virgin's singular prerogative is set in this: that she was pre-purged (προκεκάθαρται), while the other sons of Adam are said not to be pre-purged but purged. And what difference between purged and pre-purged would you find, save that in the one case purification follows the stain to remove it, in the other it forestalls to prevent the stain? So the singular privilege Sophronius here proclaims of the blessed Mother of God is nothing other than her most singular preservation from original infection. But the whole context of this passage also deserves consideration. Sophronius, evidently, as a kind of principle from which he then derives so many and such great prerogatives of the Mother of God, first puts forward what is established from the Gospel: that Mary was full of grace. And again, being about to give as it were the reason for these great things, he stresses the fullness of grace once more, and adds that immense heap of divine gifts by which the Mother of God surpasses by an infinite interval the gifts conferred on any creature. It is plain, therefore, from the mind of the holy Fathers, that both in that fullness of grace and in that excess of divine gifts above all others there is contained also the gift, common to angels and first parents, by virtue of which divine grace must be professed as coeval with her very beginning of existence.

unplaced.text: Si gratiæ munera Mariæ collata longissime excedunt quæcunque a Dei largitate in quoslibet dimanaverint; profecto aut absurdissime affirmandum est, originem peccato infectam sanctæ originis longe præcellere, aut verius fatendum est, Virginem Deiparam non modo æque ac protoparentes cœlestesque spiritus, in gratia creatam fuisse, sed longe nobilioribus gratiæ donis in eadem illa prima sui origine ex magnificentissima Dei liberalitate ac sapientia fuisse exornatam.
unplaced.anchorLine: dimanaverint (26)
unplaced.en: If the gifts of grace conferred on Mary far exceed whatever has flowed from God's bounty to anyone, then either one must most absurdly affirm that an origin infected with sin far surpasses a holy origin, or it is truer to confess that the Virgin Mother of God was not only created in grace equally with the first parents and the heavenly spirits, but was adorned at that very first origin of hers with far nobler gifts of grace from God's most magnificent liberality and wisdom.

Haud putaverim, ita hæc sensa Deiparæ a S. Sophronio tribui quasi persuasum reipsa sancto doctori fuerit, tunc sanctam Virginem hæc elocutam fuisse. Citius dixerim, more eorum, qui ex Gr. laudibus celebrantes sancti Præcursoris nativitatem, hunc utut in utero matris adhuc inclusum anticipatione quadam inducunt sublimia quæque de divinis disserentem, sic sanctum Sophronium ista de sancta Dei Genitrice pro sensis potius, quæ fidelibus inesse de eadem noverat, quam pro rei gestæ verisimilitudine protulisse, atque eadem plane de causa factum cernis, ut Gabrielis archangeli ad Virginem alloquiis illa Sophronius intermisceat, quæ ad refutandas hæreses Nestorii et Eutychetis adversus incarnationis Dominicæ mysterium opportuna videbantur, licet ea ab angelo tunc dicta fuisse, nemo sibi persuadeat.
Cæterum haud levis momenti fuerit, apud christianam plebem exploratissima tunc ea fuisse, quæ in hac Sophronii oratione legimus. Concludi enim inde potest, vulgatissimam ergo in Ecclesia doctrinam exstitisse, quæ tradit, eum locum in divina regenerationis humanæ œconomia tribuendum esse Deiparæ, qui in prima olim humani generis conditione veteri illi Evæ datus fuerat, adeo ut quæcunque primæ hujus matris propria fuerunt, ad sanctam Dei Genitricem transferenda sint. Et sane, nonne ex his Sophronii verbis patet, comparationem Mariæ inter et Evam eo usque perductam fuisse, ut sanctæ Virginis deceptio (si qua locum habuisset), et lapsus nonnisi primæ matris deceptioni et lapsui æquiparanda forent, neque minus ab illius quam hujus gestis aut rectis aut pravis universi humani generis seu sospitas seu pernicies penderet ?
Sed et ulterius aliquid ex his elucet, quod pressius ad rem præsentem spectat, nempe ex recepta tunc doctrina non aliam, ac Evæ fuerit ante lapsum, Mariæ conditionem exstitisse. Propterea hypotheticam illam sanctæ Virginis deceptionem non cum ulla ex omnigenis prævaricationibus eorum, qui in statu naturæ lapsæ versantur, sed cum Evæ errore conferri hic cernis. Propterea Virgo se comparat Evæ (sup. § 23), cum ad hanc serpens primo accessit, et quam idcirco (§ præs. paulo inf.) diserte dicit adhuc malitiæ expertem. Propterea angelus (§ 24 et 25) cum plura verset, quo testetur se non eum esse, qui in errorem ac perniciem impellat, nullas insidias memorat ac nullas ruinas, nisi quæ ad protoparentum lapsum pertinent. Huc et illud spectat, quod ejusmodi fingitur deceptio, quæ, non secus ac Evæ factum est, a divina charitate (§ 23) dejiciat : nam hæc utique idoneum sensum habent, si sanctam Virginem eo loci constitutam reputes, quem tenuit Eva ante peccatum ; contra vero nonne carent omni sensu, si Mariam quoque lapsis hominibus accenseas ? Orationis enim series non aliter lapsos homines exhibet aut exhibere hic potest (vid. a § 12 ad 18) quam peccati tenebris et umbra mortis involutos, quibus idcirco restauratio per incarnationis opus divinitus paratur ; nullus ergo locus superest divinæ gratiæ luci, e qua Maria excidere possit, siquidem ipsam quoque inter lapsos connumeres. Huc denique collineat, quod graviores adhuc ruinæ universo humano generi ex hypothetica Mariæ ruina impendere perhibeatur (§ præs.) : nunquid enim hæc palam non faciunt, ex recepta tunc doctrina veteri Evæ sic Mariam fuisse substitutam, ut, non secus atque illa, novi ordinis principium foret, novumque denuo quoddam periculum ac veluti certamen in ipsa instauraretur, cujus exitus novæ aut felicitatis aut infelicitatis origo humano generi exsisteret ? Hinc est, quod et sanctus Proclus (homilia 6, § 16) dæmones non modo consilia de sancta Virgine expugnanda tanquam de summa rerum agitantes, sed etiam expresse tanquam cum secunda Eva, æque ac prior illa, adhuc innocenti et integra bellum parantes inducat : At iterumne (inquit) cum secunda Eva nobis instat certamen ? Instruendane acies adversus impollutam mulierem ? ..... Quonam itaque modo naviculam ejusmodi tempestate jactabimus ? ..... Quonam modo discerpemus ovem ? ..... Quonam modo diripiemus civitatem ? unplaced.en: I would hardly suppose that these sentiments of the Mother of God are attributed to St. Sophronius as though the holy doctor had been actually persuaded that the holy Virgin spoke these words. I would rather say that, after the manner of those who in Greek laudations celebrate the nativity of the holy Forerunner, introducing him, though still enclosed in his mother's womb, by a kind of anticipation as discoursing on lofty divine matters, so Sophronius put these things about the holy Mother of God into her mouth rather according to the sense of what he knew the faithful held of her than for the likelihood of the event; and for the very same reason you see him mix into the angel Gabriel's words to the Virgin things that seemed suited to refuting the heresies of Nestorius and Eutyches against the mystery of the Lord's incarnation, although let no one persuade himself that these were said by the angel at that time. [Next paragraph:] It is of no slight importance that what we read in this oration was then very well known among the Christian people. For it can be concluded from this that the doctrine was very widespread in the Church which holds that the place in the divine economy of human regeneration is to be assigned to the Mother of God which in the first condition of the human race was given to that former Eve, so that whatever things were proper to this first mother are to be transferred to the holy Mother of God. And indeed, is it not plain from these words of Sophronius that the comparison between Mary and Eve was carried so far that the deception of the holy Virgin (if it had had any place), and her fall, would be equated only with the deception and fall of the first mother, and that the safety or destruction of the whole human race would depend no less on her deeds, right or wrong, than on the other's? [Next paragraph:] But something further also shines out from these words, which bears more closely on the present matter: namely that, according to the doctrine then received, Mary's condition was no other than Eve's had been before the fall. Hence you see that the hypothetical deception of the holy Virgin is compared here not with any of the manifold transgressions of those who live in the state of fallen nature, but with Eve's error. Hence the Virgin compares herself to Eve (above, § 23) when the serpent first approached her, and whom for that reason (§ present, a little below) she expressly calls still ignorant of malice. Hence the angel (§§ 24 and 25), though he treats of many things by which he testifies that he is not one who drives her into error and ruin, mentions no snares and no ruins except those pertaining to the fall of the first parents. To this too belongs the point that a deception of such kind is imagined as, no less than in Eve's case, would cast her down from divine love (§ 23): for these words make fitting sense if you consider the holy Virgin placed in the position Eve held before sin; but on the contrary do they not lack all sense if you reckon Mary also among fallen men? For the course of the oration shows fallen men, or can here show them, only as wrapped in the darkness of sin and the shadow of death (see from § 12 to 18), for whom therefore restoration is divinely prepared through the work of the incarnation; there is therefore no place left of the light of divine grace from which Mary could fall, if you number her too among the fallen. Finally this points the same way, that graver ruins are said to threaten the whole human race from the hypothetical ruin of Mary (§ present): do not these things openly show that, by the received doctrine, Mary was thus substituted for the old Eve so that, no less than she, she should be the beginning of a new order, and a new danger and, as it were, contest should be set up anew in her, the outcome of which would become for the human race the source of new happiness or unhappiness? Hence it is that St. Proclus (homily 6, § 16) represents the demons not only as planning designs against the holy Virgin as if debating the sum of things, but expressly as preparing war against one who, like the first Eve, is still innocent and whole: 'Is there then again, with the second Eve, a contest upon us? Are battle lines to be drawn against an undefiled woman? ..... In what manner then shall we toss such a little boat with tempest? ..... In what manner shall we tear the sheep apart? ..... In what manner shall we plunder the city?' But [in Greek:] 'Again for us the war is against a second one, the battle line against an incorrupt woman.' Where, that you may fully grasp the force of the words 'incorrupt woman', note what Proclus added concerning the first Eve: 'She, having shared in corruption, thought to lay hold of the higher dignity'; [Latin:] 'She, taking corruption to herself, thought she was seizing an eminent dignity.' unplaced.text: Dignum sane est, quod animadvertatur Sophronio quoque suffragante, non ex absoluta rei necessitate, sed ex decentia repetendum esse, quod Verbum Dei Filius, carnem humanam assumens, e matre Virgine præter naturæ ordinem nasci voluerit. Quæ quidem doctrina explorata adeo et scholæ theologis fuit, ut eximius Suarez (in part. III, q. 22, disp. 10, sect. 3), cum hanc thesim statuisset : Dicendum vero est, absque ulla dubitatione, potuisse Deum hominem concipi et generari ex muliere opera viri ; continuo subdat : Hanc assertionem censeo adeo certam, ut contraria nec probabilis nec verisimilis sit. Exinde vero liquet, haud rem acu eos tangere, qui putant, ideo ejusmodi conceptionis rationem in Christo repugnasse, quod repugnet, Christum originali Adæ peccato inflici potuisse, atque hinc permoveri se affirmant, ne Virginem Deiparam, quæ consueto naturæ ordine concepta est, ab Adamitico peccato exemptam fuisse existiment. Etiam si, inquit idem Suarez (in III part., quæst. 15, disp. 33, sect. 2), per seminalem propagationem conciperetur (Christus), si supponamus factam esse unionem a primo instanti conceptionis ejus, etiam non posset ex vi talis conceptionis peccatum originale contrahere. Curnam vero ? Quia scilicet non adeo necessarius est nexus inter generationem ab Adam ordinario modo deductam et originalem labem, ut hæc duo invicem sejungi, Deo sic dispensante, non queant. Hinc et illa nonnulorum Patrum sententia, sanctum Domini Præcursorem, quem nemo certe credidit sine seminali propagatione conceptum, ab originis vitio fuisse præservatum.
unplaced.anchorLine: veniebat etiam, atque ipsi debebatur, (37) ut, remoto
unplaced.en: It is worth noting that Sophronius too supports the view that the reason why the Word, the Son of God, taking human flesh, willed to be born of a Virgin mother beyond the order of nature is to be sought not in absolute necessity of the matter but in fittingness. This doctrine was so well explored even in the theologians' school that the eminent Suárez (part III, q. 22, disp. 10, sect. 3), having laid down the thesis 'It must be said, without any doubt, that God could have been conceived as man and generated of a woman by the act of a man,' at once adds: 'I judge this assertion so certain that the contrary is neither probable nor likely.' From this it is plain that those miss the point who think that such a manner of conception was repugnant in Christ because Christ could then have been tainted with Adam's original sin, and who say that they are moved by this so as not to suppose that the Virgin Mother of God, who was conceived in the customary order of nature, was exempt from Adamic sin. 'Even if,' says the same Suárez (part III, q. 15, disp. 33, sect. 2), 'Christ were conceived by seminal propagation, supposing the union made from the first instant of his conception, he still could not contract original sin by force of such a conception.' Why so? Because the link between generation derived from Adam in the ordinary way and the original stain is not so necessary that these two cannot be separated, God so ordaining. Hence also the opinion of some of the Fathers that the holy Forerunner of the Lord, whom surely no one believed to be conceived without seminal propagation, was preserved from the taint of origin.

Manifeste hic Sophronius docet, hunc quoque errorem Nestorio tribuendum, quod Dominicæ carnis seu naturæ humanæ exsistentiam non contemporaneam qualicunque, quam admisit, conjunctioni cum Deo Verbo, sed plane huic præcedentem tradiderit. Et ne putes, his Samosatensem Paulum (qui § seq. simul cum Nestorio ac Theodoro memoratur) potius quam Nestorium impeti, vides quæ eadem de re Sophronius habet in celeberrima sua Synodica (supra) : Σαρκοῦται γοῦν Λόγος ὁ Θεός, ... οὐ προπλασθείσῃ σαρκὶ συναπτόμενος, ἢ προμορφωθέντι καὶ καθ᾽ αὑτὸ προϋποστάντι ποτὲ προσπλεκόμενος σώματι ... ἀλλὰ τότε τούτοις παραγενομένοις πρὸς ὕπαρξιν, ὅτε αὐτοῖς ὁ Λόγος ... συνετίθετο · φυσικῶς σύγχρονον ἔχοντα τῇ ὑπάρξει τὴν ἕνωσιν, καὶ οὐ πρὸ τῆς πρὸς τὸν Λόγον ἀληθεστάτης συμβάσεως καθ᾽ ἑαυτὰ γενόμενα πώποτε ... ἀλλὰ σύνδρομον ἔχοντα τῇ φυσικῇ τοῦ Λόγου συμβάσει τὴν ὕπαρξιν, καὶ οὐκ ἐκείνης, οὐδὲ ὡς ἐν ὀφθαλμοῦ ῥιπῇ ταύτην προτερεύουσαν ἔχοντα, ὡς Παῦλος ὁ Σαμοσατεὺς βομβεῖ καὶ Νεστόριος. Ἅμα γὰρ σάρξ, ἅμα Θεοῦ Λόγου σάρξ, κ. τ. λ. Incarnatur ergo Verbum Dei, ... non præformatæ carni semel coaptans, aut præformato corpori aliquando in se subsistenti se conjungens, sed his ad exsistentiam tunc venientibus, quando ipse Deus Verbum eisdem copulabatur : naturalem nempe unionem habent contemporaneam exsistentiæ, non vero exstiterunt in se aliquando ante verissimum cum Verbo conventum : ... sed synchronam naturali Verbi conjunctioni exsistentiam habent, non autem, ut Samosatensis Paulus ac Nestorius perstrepit, hanc illi tempore præcedentem habent, ne ictu quidem oculi. Simul quippe caro, simul Verbi Dei caro, etc.
Porro hæc quoque conferre debent ad abstergendam labem qua inconsulto vel sanctus pontifex Leo M. aspergitur. Scilicet cum Leo quoque et apertissime et sæpius (vid. epist. 59, ad cler. et pleb. Constantinop., cap. 5, epist. 102, ad episc. Galliar., cap. 3, et serm. 28, in Nativ. Dom., 8, cap. 5, edit. Baller.) Nestorium vitiati dogmatis circa tempus unionis Verbi cum carne incuset, jam si vera est sententia Joannis Garnerii (De hær. et libr. Nestor., diss. 1, § 3, pag. 286), de unionis tempore Nestorium ab Ecclesiæ sententia non recessisse, eo res adducitur, ut sanctus doctor insigni imprudentia (ne temeritate dicamus, aut calumnia) falsum Nestorio crimen dicendus sit imposuisse. Atqui hoc ipsum morari Garnerium debuit, ne præceps eam in opinionem veniret. Quid enim ? Nonne sanctus Leo quo tempore controversia Nestoriana agitabatur, sancti Cœlestini lateri, utpote Romanæ Ecclesiæ archidiaconus, assidebat, primasque in gerendis negotiis partes agebat ? Nonne sanctus Leo, [blotted: ?quod] Garnerius non diffitetur, ad manus habuit Nestorii scripta, etiam ea e quibus suam Garnerius opinionem firmat, quæ et refutanda ad Joannem Cassianum ante ipsam synodum Ephesinam transmisit ? Nonne, cum synodus Ephesina celebraretur, ad Leonem Cyrillus de gravissimis concilii negotiis, quo ad sanctum Cœlestinum deferrentur, scribebat ? Cuinam vero e Romano clero, vel quandonam apostolicæ sedi perspectas Nestorii res affirmabimus, si tunc incompertas putemus sancto Leoni, qui propterea tam crasse erraverit, atque insuper ad affirmanda ea, de quibus ignorabat, temere progressus fuerit ?
Miratur Garnerius (l. c.) hominum aliud Nestorio tribuentium sententiam. Atqui mirandum potius, quod tam facile sibi ipse suaserit, tot viros doctrina et sanctitate præclaros, quorum prolixum catalogum tum ex Oriente, tum ex Occidente, si locus ferret, facile foret subjicere, et quorum multi coævi factis fuerunt, nihil aut certe minus, quam ipse viderit, de hac re pervidisse, ac tenere scripsisse. Præsertim vero, quod summa argumentorum pro ea sententia in verbis demum Nestorii sita sit, ut merito domui in summa arena fundatæ comparari queat. Nunquid enim ea Nestorii dicta evincunt, ipsum aliter docuisse nunquam ? Sane ut id affirmes, unica tibi præsto est ratio, ut Nestorii in doctrinis semel prolatis constantiam vindices. Atqui occurret tibi sanctus Cœlestinus, quo auctore (Epist. ad Nestor., n. 2) Nestorius vera involvens obscuris, rursus utraque confundens, vel confitetur negata, vel nititur negare confessa ; occurret tibi et Marius Mercator, lectorem monens (Dissert. de XII anathem. Nest., n. 22), ut cautus sit de Nestorii varietate et inconstantia, quam, ait, utrum astutia an vecordia ad alliciendum auditorem habeat, non est facile nosse : quovis tamen pacto constat, eum varium esse, sibique contrarium. Agitur ergo de re judicata : ac tantumdem constantiæ Nestorii deferre licet, quantum fidei tribuere consuevimus hominis testimonio, qui solemni judicio maxime mendacissimus fuerit proclamatus. Non adeo ergo de ea constantia præsumendum fuit, ut tot Patres antiqui, quibus nemo unus e veteribus contradixerat, inscitiæ damnarentur.
Cæterum aliqua Garnerio excusatio ex eo non defuerit, quod Petavius, quem oppugnandum sibi proposuit, leviuscule hoc argumentum pertractaverat. Quod Cyrillus ejusmodi errorem non reprehenderit. Jam enim ab anno 1833 Em. Maius sancti Cy-

unplaced.en:
Sophronius plainly teaches here that this error too is to be ascribed to Nestorius: that he handed down the existence of the Lord's flesh, or human nature, as not contemporaneous with whatever union with God the Word he admitted, but as plainly preceding it. And lest you think that Paul of Samosata (who is named with Nestorius and Theodore in the following section) rather than Nestorius is attacked here, see what Sophronius says on the same matter in his celebrated Synodica (above): 'The Word, God, is incarnate, ... not joined to flesh previously fashioned, nor interwoven with a body previously formed and ever self-subsisting ... but when these came into being, when the Word ... was composed with them: having the union naturally simultaneous with existence, and never having come into being by themselves before the truest conjunction with the Word ... but having their existence running together with the Word's natural conjunction, and not having it precede that, not even in the blink of an eye, as Paul of Samosata and Nestorius babble. For at once flesh, at once the flesh of God the Word,' etc. [Latin version:] 'The Word of God is incarnated, not joining himself once to flesh already formed, or to a body previously subsisting in itself, but these coming to existence at the moment God the Word was joined to them ... not, as Paul of Samosata and Nestorius shout, having this existence precede in time, not even by a moment. At once flesh, at once the flesh of the Word of God,' etc.
Moreover these things should also help wipe away the stain with which the holy pontiff Leo the Great is thoughtlessly spattered. For since Leo, too, both most openly and repeatedly (see letter 59, to the clergy and people of Constantinople, ch. 5; letter 102, to the bishops of Gaul, ch. 3; and sermon 28, on the Nativity of the Lord, 8, ch. 5, Ballerini ed.) accuses Nestorius of a corrupt doctrine about the time of the union of the Word with flesh, then, if Joannes Garnerius's view is true (On the heresies and books of Nestorius, diss. 1, § 3, p. 286) that Nestorius did not depart from the Church's view on the time of the union, matters come to this: that the holy doctor must be said, with remarkable imprudence (not to say rashness or calumny), to have imposed a false charge on Nestorius. Yet this very thing should have held Garnerius back from rushing into that opinion. For what? At the time the Nestorian controversy was in agitation, did not St. Leo, as archdeacon of the Roman Church, sit at St. Celestine's side and take the leading part in conducting business? Did not St. Leo, as Garnerius does not deny, have in hand the writings of Nestorius, even those from which Garnerius confirms his opinion, which he also sent to John Cassian to be refuted before the Council of Ephesus itself? Did not Cyril write to Leo, while the Council of Ephesus was being held, about the gravest business of the council, to be brought to St. Celestine? Whose affairs of Nestorius, then, among the Roman clergy, or when, shall we affirm to have been clearly known to the Apostolic See, if we suppose them unknown to St. Leo, who on that account erred so grossly and, further, rashly proceeded to affirm things of which he was ignorant?
Garnerius wonders at the opinion of men who attribute a different view to Nestorius. But rather it is wonderful that he so easily persuaded himself that so many men renowned for learning and holiness (whose long catalogue, East and West alike, it would be easy to append if space allowed, and many of whom were contemporaries) saw nothing in this matter, or at least less than he has seen, and wrote with understanding; especially since the sum of the arguments for that view rests only on Nestorius's words, so that it might justly be compared to a house built on the top of sand. Do those sayings of Nestorius prove that he never taught otherwise? To affirm that, the only ground you have is to vindicate Nestorius's constancy in the doctrines once set forth. But there will confront you St. Celestine, on whose authority (Letter to Nestorius, n. 2) Nestorius 'involving truths in obscurities, again confounding both, either confesses what he denied or strives to deny what he confessed'; and there will confront you Marius Mercator, warning the reader (Dissertation on the 12 anathemas of Nestorius, n. 22) to be 'wary of Nestorius's variability and inconstancy, which, he says, whether he has by craft or by madness to entice the hearer, is not easy to know: by any means, however, it is certain that he is changeable and self-contradictory.' The matter is therefore already judged: and we may grant to Nestorius's constancy only as much as we are wont to give of credence to the testimony of a man who has been proclaimed by solemn judgment most mendacious. It was therefore not so far to be presumed on that constancy that so many ancient Fathers, whom no one of the ancients had contradicted, should be condemned for ignorance.
Besides, some excuse for Garnerius may exist in that Petavius, whom he set himself to oppose, had handled this argument rather lightly. But now there is the less room for doubt, as the two little arguments Garnerius added for his own case collapse the more surely: namely 1. that Nestorius constantly called Mary Christotokos (Χριστοτόκος); 2. that Cyril did not reprehend such an error. For already since the year 1833 His Eminence Mai [published] St. Cy[ril] ... [note breaks off at foot of page; continues on the next page].

unplaced.en: A more common inflexion of the name of Manes among the Greeks is Μάνης, Μάνους; for so, to cite some, Cyril of Jerusalem (Catech. VI, n. 24), Nazianzen (orat. 25, al. 23, § 8), Nyssen (Against Eunomius, orat. 10), Chrysostom (On Virginity, § 3), Epiphanius (heresy 66, § 1, 2), Damascene (On Heresies, § 66). Eusebius of Caesarea, however (Eccl. Hist. book VII, ch. 31), bending the name to suit Manes's character, uses the form Μάνεις [as printed], as if he were so called from μαίνομαι (I am mad), inasmuch as, as he adds, he was 'by his very nature mad' and 'puffed up over his madness.' For the same cause, although Socrates (Eccl. Hist. book I, ch. 22) wrote of Manes 'he renames himself Manes' (he once calls himself Manes), yet in the title of that same chapter we read 'On Manentes' (περὶ τοῦ Μανέντος). You have both forms equally in the History of the Manichaeans composed by Peter of Sicily, in which (n. 41, in Mai, Nova Patrum Bibliotheca, vol. IV, part 2, p. 15) both 'ill-named Mantes' (Manes of ill-omened name) occurs, and (n. 21, p. 29) 'Constantine, disciple of Manes' (τοῦ Μανέντος μαθητής), although Peter, no differently from Socrates, writes (n. 12, p. 17): 'instead of Cubricus he named himself Manes' (pro Cubrico he named himself Manes). But Nicetas Choniates (On the Manichaeans, in Mai, ibid., p. 110) uses the form Μανέντα, where he also treats of the name assumed by Manes: 'For he was formerly called Cubricus, then renamed himself Manentas' (he was formerly called Cubricus; then named himself Manes); though another form is also found in the same Nicetas, who soon adds: 'Manes signifies in the language of the Babylonians a vessel' (Manes means in the language of the Babylonians a vase). Indeed in Theodoret (Fabulae haereticorum, book I, ch. 26) one sees not only Μάνης and Μανέντος, but by a third inflexion εἰς Μάνητα. Let this be noted so that it may be clear to what end Sophronius used the form Μανέντες, which Saint Maximus also used in the same age, where (vol. II, p. 18) he reproaches Severus that he also taught the 'phantasy of Manes' (Μανέντος φαντασίαν).

unplaced.en: We have this oration from the library of Maximus Margunius. It was translated into Latin long ago by Achilles Statius, a Portuguese, whose version was sent to me from Rome by Fr Hieronymus Brunellus, priest of our Society, after I had made this new one. The author of this oration is Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem, whose anniversary Greeks and Latins keep on 2 March. The Greeks give this eulogy: 'Of our holy father Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem, of Damascus by birth, distinguished by manifold learning, knowledge of the divine writings and piety. He flourished under Heraclius, in whose 19th year he was raised to that see and died in the 28th: When, as Cedrenus says, he had long and much contended against Heraclius and Sergius and Pyrrhus the Monothelites who agreed with him,' and had left many writings to the Church, among them the book entitled Pratum spirituale; the Life of Mary of Egypt, various encomia on saints, two homilies on the cross; and the synodical Epistle to Pope John and to Sergius, bishop of Constantinople. See Cedrenus and Zonaras on Heraclius. Sophronius delivered this oration on the eve of the Exaltation of the holy Cross, i.e. 13 September, the day on which the dedication of the temple at Jerusalem, called the Anastasis or Resurrection, is celebrated. The Typicon of Sabas, on the 13th day: 'The dedication of the holy Resurrection of Christ our God.' And in this whole oration Sophronius speaks of this resurrection, not of the feast of the Resurrection or Easter.

so-019: Sophronium hunc posteriorem esse priore illo altero cujus ut presbyteri meminit, descripsitque vitam sanctus Hieronymus in Scriptorum ecclesiasticorum catalogo : cum ille sancto Hieronymo σύγχρονος ad tempora Joannis 44 Hierosolymitani pontificis vixerit. Hic vero cum in sua de Christi natalitiis oratione multis agat de immani sævaque tyrannide Saracenorum qui per id tempus oppidum Bethleem occupabant, satis indicat se illum esse Sophronium 62, ac postremum Pontificem Hierosolymitanum, cujus meminit Nicephori Constantinopolitani Chronologia. Pleniora de S. Sophronio Hierosolymitano episcopo suppeditabit tomo VIII Annalium ecclesiasticorum exact. 13, sextæ synodi ex concilio Romano sub S. Martino Papa, secretario 2, tomo III. Ex Theophane in Miscella et aliis. Consule quoque notas ad Romanum Martyrologium 11 Martii. Consignatur obitus sancti Sophronii sub Heraclio imperatore, anno salutis 636, 11 Martii, quo die ejus natalis inter sanctos inscriptus habetur publicis Latinæ et Græcæ Ecclesiæ tabulis. Bibliotheca Patrum, t. XII, 206.

That this Sophronius is the later one, distinct from the earlier one whom Jerome mentions as a presbyter and whose life he wrote in his catalogue of ecclesiastical writers (Jerome being a contemporary of the Jerusalem bishop John), is clear: for in this oration on Christ's Nativity he speaks at length of the savage tyranny of the Saracens who at that time held Bethlehem, which shows that he is the Sophronius who was the last Patriarch of Jerusalem and who is mentioned in the Chronology of Nicephorus of Constantinople. Fuller details on St Sophronius will be given in volume VIII of the Annales ecclesiastici (year 13 [sic as printed: exact. 13]), in the acts of the sixth synod from the Roman council under St Martin the Pope (secretary 2, vol. III), from Theophanes in the Miscella, and others. See also the notes to the Roman Martyrology at 11 March. The death of St Sophronius is recorded under Emperor Heraclius, in the year of salvation 636, on 11 March, the day on which his feast is entered among the saints in the public tables of the Latin and Greek Church. Bibliotheca Patrum, vol. XII, 206.
Attexuntur huic quædam etiam de immani sævaque Saracenorum tyrannide, qui per id tempus oppidum Bethleem, vel occuparant, vel certe obsessum tenebant.
Some remarks are also woven into this oration about the savage and monstrous tyranny of the Saracens, who at that time had either occupied the town of Bethlehem or at least held it besieged.

Eudoxius Arianus Constantinopolitanæ invasor sedis baptizavit Valentem imperatorem, cui se adjunxit Aetius magister Eunomii, dein ab Eudoxio constituti episcopi Cyziceni, quem expulsum apud se Constantinopoli detinuit. Ita Socr. l. IV, c. 1 et 7, et S. Epiphan. hæres. 75, n. 38, qui hæreticis Anomæis annumerat, quorum princeps Eunomius habebatur.

Eudoxius the Arian, usurper of the see of Constantinople, baptised the emperor Valens, to whom Aetius, the teacher of Eunomius, attached himself, and who was afterwards appointed bishop of Cyzicus by Eudoxius, who kept him with himself at Constantinople when he was expelled. So Socrates, book 4, chs. 1 and 7, and St. Epiphanius, heresy 75 [sic, as I read it], n. 38, who reckons him among the Anomoean heretics, whose leader Eunomius was held to be.

Asterius Sophista in persecutione Maximiani Christianam fidem ejuravit. S. Epiphan. hæres. 76, n. 3. Agunt de eo homine Cappadoce et Ariano, ejusque libris Socr. l. I, c. 24 ; Sozom. l. II, c. 31 ; S. Athanasius De Synodo, aliique.

Asterius the Sophist abjured the Christian faith in the persecution of Maximian. St. Epiphanius, heresy 76, n. 3. Socrates, book 1, ch. 24; Sozomen, book 2, ch. 31; St. Athanasius On the Synod, and others, treat of this man, a Cappadocian and an Arian, and of his books.

Apollinaris Laodiceni hæreses describit Epiphan. hæresi 77, n. 22 ; scilicet Christum corpus e cœlo detulisse, animam non assumpsisse, corpus divinitati consubstantiale fuisse. Agit de eo Sozomen. l. VI, c. 25, et alii : eum S. Damasus papa Romæ in synodo damnavit anno 373.

Epiphanius describes the heresies of Apollinaris of Laodicea in heresy 77, n. 22: namely that Christ brought a body from heaven, did not assume a soul, and that the body was consubstantial with the divinity. Sozomen, book 6, ch. 25, and others treat of him: Pope St. Damasus condemned him at Rome in a synod in the year 373.

Severus sedem Antiochenam expulso S. Flaviano per vim invasit anno 513, ex secta Acephalorum, oppugnator concil. Chalcedonensis. Coluntur SS. Flavianus, et Elias tunc quoque per ipsum e sede Hierosolymitana pulsus, 4 Julii.

Severus seized the see of Antioch by force in the year 513, St. Flavian having been expelled; he was of the sect of the Acephali and an opponent of the Council of Chalcedon. SS. Flavian, and Elias, who was likewise then driven from the see of Jerusalem by him, are honoured on 4 July.

Dioscorus episcopus Alexandrinus patronus Eutychetis, cum eo in concilio Chalcedonensi damnatus. De eo agemus 18 Febr. ad Vitam S. Flaviani episcopi Constantinopolitani, ab ejus factionis hominibus in exsilium pulsi.

Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, patron of Eutyches, was condemned together with him at the Council of Chalcedon. We shall treat of him on 18 February, in the Life of St. Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, who was driven into exile by men of his faction.

Cum Petrus Moggus in sedem Alexandrinam anno 482 receptus, Henotico Zenonis imperatoris admisso, Catholicos simul et hæreticos offendisset, Eutychiani plures ab utrisque deficientes, Acephali, id est, sine capite sunt appellati : in varias mox sectas divisi.

When Peter Mongus, received into the see of Alexandria in the year 482 on the admission of the emperor Zeno's Henoticon, had offended Catholics and heretics alike, many Eutychians, falling away from both sides, were called Acephali, that is, 'headless': they were soon divided into various sects.
Polemonem ex scriptis Apollinarii ansam nactum, dixisse in Christo substantiarum confusionem factam, et commistionem divinitatis et corporis tradit Theodoretus, l. IV Hæret. fabul. cap. 9.

Theodoret (Haereticarum fabularum book 4, ch. 9) reports that Polemon, having taken occasion from Apollinaris's writings, said that a confusion of substances was made in Christ, and a commingling of divinity and body.

Ebion princeps hæresis, quæ Christum nudum hominem appellavit, contra quem et Cerinthum S. Joannes suum Evangelium scripsit. Agunt de eo Theodoretus in compendio hæreticarum fabularum, earumque lib. II, cap. 1 ; S. Epiphanius hæresi 51, aliique.

Ebion, chief of the heresy which called Christ a mere man, against whom and against Cerinthus St. John wrote his Gospel. Theodoret treats of him in his compendium of heretical fables, book 2, ch. 1; St. Epiphanius, heresy 51, and others.
De Paulo Samosateno agit S. Ephræm Syrus in Testamento quo Bardesanem strenue confutatum esse tradit Theodoretus lib. I Hær. fab., cap. 22 ; de hoc etiam agit S. Epiphanius hæresi 22.

St. Ephrem the Syrian treats of Paul of Samosata in his Testament, in which, Theodoret reports (Haer. fab. book 1, ch. 22), Bardesanes is vigorously refuted; St. Epiphanius also treats of him, heresy 22.
